problem_data.story:
I nearly tripped over the kid in the dark before I saw her.

Her hoverchair was parked as usual on the narrow strip of synthetic grass that separated her mother's housing pod from the one Daniel Wallace and I lived in, but it wasn't exactly where I'd learned to expect it when I rolled in at night from the biotech labs. Usually it was nearer the west end of the strip where Emily could look across the transparent aluminum square of the Foxwood City residential complex and the biodiversity conservation zones to the maglev transit line beyond. But this time it was pushed back into the shadows away from the complex lights.

The girl wasn't watching the conservation zones tonight, as she usually did. Instead she was lying back in her chair with her face turned to the holographic display floating above her, staring upward with such absorbed intensity that she didn't even know I was there until I spoke.

"Anything wrong, Emily?" I asked.

She said, "No, Logan," without taking her eyes off the display.

For a minute I had the prickly feeling you get when you are watching a simulation and find that you know just what is going to happen next. You're puzzled and a little spooked until you realize that the reason you can predict the action so exactly is because you've seen the same thing happen somewhere else a long time ago. I forgot the feeling when I remembered why the kid wasn't watching the conservation zones. But I couldn't help wondering why she'd turned to manipulating molecular structures instead.

"What're you working on up there, Emily?" I asked.

She didn't move and from the tone of her voice I got the impression that she only half heard me.

"I'm rearranging some proteins," she said softly.

I gave it up and went on to my own pod without asking any more fool questions. How can you talk to a kid like that?

Our pod was dark inside. I switched on the light and dumped my packages on the counter, noting the empty flavor enhancer containers scattered by the synthesizer—Daniel's calling cards when he'd been at loose ends. The pattern was familiar: dark pod, empties on the counter, and usually an empty bunk with Daniel having wandered off somewhere. But this time he was actually there, asleep in his bunk, which threw me.

The smell hit me when I shook him awake—synthetic whiskey, the cheap kind from the dispensaries on the east side of Foxwood City. That part fit the pattern well enough. But what made me look twice was that at some time during the day he had bathed and groomed himself. He had even cleaned and pressed a shirt; it hung on a hook over his bunk with a crumpled pack of vapor sticks in the pocket.

Daniel sat up and blinked against the light, a thin, elderly man with bright blue eyes, a clipped gray beard and scanty gray hair tousled and wild from sleep. He was stripped to his undergarments against the heat, looking more presentable than he had in weeks.

"Crawl out and prepare dinner, Rip," I said, holding him to his end of our working agreement. "I've made a shift and I'm hungry."

Daniel got up and stepped into his pants. He padded barefoot across the floor and poked at the packages on the counter.

"Synthesized protein again," he complained. "Logan, I'm sick of this stuff!"

"You don't catch real meat with a basic income credit," I told him. And because I'd never been able to stay sore at him for long I added, "But we got flavor enhancers. Where's the dispenser?"

"I'm sick of flavor enhancers, too," Daniel said. "I need a real drink."

I sniffed the air, making a business of it. "You've had one already. Where?"

He grinned at me then with the wise-to-himself-and-the-world grin that lit up his face like turning on a light inside and made him different from anybody else on earth.

"The largess of Providence," he said, "is bestowed impartially upon sot and Samaritan. I helped the little one next door to the bathroom this afternoon while her mother was away at work, and my selflessness had its just reward."

Sometimes it's hard to tell when Daniel is kidding. He's an educated man—used to teach at some Northern university, he said once, and I never doubted it—and talks like one when he wants to. He still carried traces of that polish from his academic days, though you'd never know it most of the time. Daniel's no bum, though he's a semi-alcoholic and lets me support him like an invalid uncle, and he's keen enough to read my mind like a data stream.

"No, I didn't break into the cupboard and help myself," he said. "The lady—her name is Camila Gutierrez—gave me the drink. Why else do you suppose I'd clean a shirt?"

That was like Daniel. He hadn't touched her bottle though his insides were probably snarled up like corrupted code for the want of it. He'd groomed and pressed a shirt instead so he'd look decent enough to rate a shot of whiskey she'd offer him as a reward. It wasn't such a doubtful gamble at that, because Daniel has a way with him when he bothers to use it; maybe that's why he bums around with me after the lab work and temporary gigs, because he's used that charm too often in the wrong places.

"Good enough," I said and activated a nutrition packet apiece for us while Daniel put the protein to heat.

He told me more about our neighbors while we consumed the packets. The Gutierrezes were permanent residents. The kid—her name was Emily and she was ten—was a genetic disorder case who hadn't walked for over a year, and her mother was a server at a food dispensary named the Coral Shell. There wasn't any Mr. Gutierrez. I guessed there never had been, which would explain why Camila acted so tough and sullen.

I was getting used to this cleaned-up version of Daniel—it seemed like a lot of effort for one drink, but that was his business. We were halfway through dinner when I remembered something the kid had said.

"Who's Rita?" I asked.

Daniel frowned at his plate. "The kid had a therapy companion named Rita, an advanced AI construct with only one optical sensor functioning and no affection protocols for anybody but the girl. The companion isn't coming home. It was destroyed by a transport vehicle on the transit line while Emily was hospitalized with her condition."

"Tough," I said, thinking of the kid sitting out there all day in her hoverchair, straining her eyes across the conservation zones. "You mean she's been waiting a year?"

Daniel nodded, seemed to lose interest in the Gutierrezes, so I let the subject drop. We sat around after dinner and consumed the rest of the flavor enhancers. When we turned in around midnight I figured we wouldn't be staying long at the Foxwood City residential complex. It wasn't a very comfortable place.

I was wrong there. It wasn't comfortable, but we stayed.

I couldn't have said at first why we stuck, and if Daniel could he didn't volunteer. Neither of us talked about it. We just went on living the way we were used to living, a few weeks here and a few there, all over the colonies.

We'd hit the Foxwood City sector too late for the agricultural biotech season, so I went in for the protein synthesis labs instead. I worked the labs all the way from Foxwood City down to Valleyview, Wendria, not signing on with any of the major corporations because I like to move quick when I get restless. I picked the independent cellular engineering runs mostly, because the percentage is good there if you've got steady hands and sharp eyes.

Cellular engineering isn't the career planning opportunity it seems to the one-shift workers who flock along because the credit is decent. You work in a sterile lab, usually, with neural interfaces instead of regular equipment, and you use multiple monitoring systems that go down to the molecular level where the complex structures are. There's no real thrill to it, as the one-shift workers find out quickly. A protein synthesis puts up no more challenge than basic assembly and the biggest job is to maintain quality control once you've got your batch stabilized.

Usually a pro like me sells his output to the lab's owner or to some clumsy worker who wants his metrics boosted, and there's nearly always a bonus—from a pool made up at the beginning of every cycle—for the person producing the highest quality batch of the day. There's a knack to engineering the complex ones, and when the bonuses were running good I only worked a shift or so a week and spent the rest of the time lying around the pod playing strategy games and consuming flavor enhancers with Daniel Wallace.

Usually it was the life of Riley, but somehow it wasn't enough in this place. We'd get about half-intoxicated and work up a promising argument about healthcare policy or ethical decision-making in biotechnology. Then, just when we'd got life looking its screwball funniest with our arguments one or the other of us would look out the window and see Emily Gutierrez in her hoverchair, waiting for an AI companion named Rita to come floating home across the biodiversity conservation zones. She was always there, day or night, until her mother came home from work and guided her inside.

It wasn't right or natural for a kid to wait like that for anything and it worried me. I even offered once to buy the kid another companion but Camila Gutierrez told me quick to mind my own business. Daniel explained that the kid didn't want another companion because she had what Daniel called a psychological block.

"Rita was more than just an AI to her," Daniel said. "She was a sort of symbol because she offered the kid two things that no one else in the world could—security and independence. With Rita keeping her company she felt secure, and she was independent of the kids who could run and play because she had Rita to interact with. If she took another companion now she'd be giving up more than Rita. She'd be giving up everything that Rita had meant to her, then there wouldn't be any point in living."

I could see it when Daniel put it that way. The companion had spent more time with Emily than Camila had, and the kid felt as safe with it as she'd have been with a security detail. And Rita, being a single-user AI, had depended on Emily for the interaction protocols she wouldn't execute for anybody else. The companion needed Emily and Emily needed her. Together, they'd been a natural.

At first I thought it was funny that Emily never complained or cried when Rita didn't come home, but Daniel explained that it was all a part of this psychological block business. If Emily cried she'd be admitting that Rita was lost. So she waited and watched, secure in her belief that Rita would return.

The Gutierrezes got used to Daniel and me being around, but they never got what you'd call intimate. Emily would laugh at some of the droll things Daniel said, but her eyes always went back to the conservation zones and the transit line, looking for Rita. And she never let anything interfere with her routine.

That routine started every morning when old Fernando Simpson, the delivery coordinator, piloted his drone out from Foxwood City to leave a handful of packages for the residential complex tenants. Fernando would always make it a point to route back by way of the Gutierrez pod and Emily would stop him and ask if he'd seen anything of a one-sensor AI companion on his route that day.

Old Fernando would lean against his control panel and deactivate his visor, scowling while he pretended to think.

Then he'd say, "Not today, Emily," or, "Thought so yesterday, but this one had two sensors on it. 'Twasn't Rita."

Then he'd pilot away, shaking his head. Later on the maintenance worker would come around to swap waste processors under the pods and Emily would ask him the same question. Once a month the power company sent out a technician to read the energy meters and he was part of Emily's routine too.

It was hard on Camila. Sometimes the kid would dream at night that Rita had come home and was signaling at the pod entrance to be let in, and she'd wake Camila and beg her to go out and see. When that happened Daniel and I could hear Camila talking to her, low and steady, until all hours of the morning, and when she finally went back to sleep we'd hear her open the cupboard and take out the whiskey bottle.

But there came a night that was more than Camila could take, a night that changed Emily's routine and a lot more with it. It left a mark you've seen yourself—everybody has that's got eyes to see—though you never knew what made it. Nobody ever knew that but Emily and Camila Gutierrez and Daniel and me.

Daniel and I were turning in around midnight that night when the kid sang out next door. We heard Camila get up and go to her, and we got up too and activated a flavor enhancer because we knew neither of us would sleep any more till she got Emily quiet again. But this night was different. Camila hadn't talked to the kid long when she yelled, "Rita! Rita!" and after that we heard both of them crying.

A little later Camila came out into the artificial moonlight and shut the pod door behind her. She looked rumpled and beaten, her hair straggling damply on her shoulders and her eyes puffed and red from crying. The whiskey she'd had hadn't helped any either.

She stood for a while without moving, then she looked up at the sky and said something I'm not likely to forget.

"Why couldn't You give the kid a break?" she said, not railing or anything but loud enough for us to hear. "You, up there—what's another lousy one-sensor AI to You?"

Daniel and I looked at each other in the half-dark of our own pod. "She's done it, Logan," Daniel said.

I knew what he meant and wished I didn't. Camila had finally told the kid that Rita wasn't coming back, not ever.

That's why I was worried about Emily when I came home the next evening and found her manipulating molecular structures instead of watching the conservation zones. It meant she'd given up waiting for Rita. And the quiet way the kid spoke of rearranging proteins worried me more, because it sounded outright impossible.

Not that you could blame her for going off her head. It was tough enough to be pinned to a hoverchair without being able to wiggle so much as a toe. But to lose her companion in the bargain....

I was on my third flavor enhancer when Daniel Wallace rolled in with a big package under his arm. The look of him stopped me—clear-eyed and steady on his feet, carrying himself with something of that old professorial bearing he'd let slip years ago. He was hot and tired from a shopping trip to Springfield District, which itself was unusual enough. It was when he unpacked his package, though, that I thought he'd lost his mind.

"Educational materials for Emily," Daniel said. "Camila and I agreed this morning that the girl needs another interest to occupy her time now, and since she can't go to school I'm going to teach her here."

He went on to explain that Camila hadn't had the heart the night before, desperate as she was, to tell the kid the whole truth. She'd told her instead, quoting an imaginary customer at the Coral Shell, that a transport vehicle with off-world registration had picked Rita up on the transit line and taken her away. It was a good enough story. Emily still didn't know that Rita was destroyed, but her waiting was over because no AI could be expected to find its way home from off-world.

"We've got to give the girl another interest," Daniel said, putting away the materials and activating another flavor enhancer. "Emily has a remarkable talent for concentration—most handicapped children have—that could be the end of her if it isn't diverted into safe channels."

I thought the kid had cracked up already and said so.

"Rearranging proteins?" Daniel said when I told him. "Good Lord, Logan—"

Camila Gutierrez knocked just then, interrupting him. She came in and had a flavor enhancer with us and talked to Daniel about his plan for educating Emily at home. But she couldn't tell us anything more about the kid's new fixation than we already knew. When she asked her why she manipulated molecular structures like that she'd say only that she wants something to remember Rita by.

It was about nine o'clock, when Camila went home to prepare supper. Daniel and I knocked off our strategy game and went outside with our portable chairs to get some air. It was then that the first protein structure changed.

It changed all of a sudden, the way any cellular mutation does, and transformed across the holographic display in a curving, blue-white cascade of molecular bonds. I didn't pay much attention, but Daniel nearly choked on his flavor enhancer.

"Logan," he said, "that was a hemoglobin variant! It mutated! Spontaneously!"

I didn't see anything spontaneous about it and said so. You can see a dozen or so protein structures shift across a display on any work cycle if you're in the mood to look.

"Not just shift, you fool," Daniel said. "The structure hemoglobin—a critical oxygen transport protein—it mutated a good sixty degrees in its quaternary structure, then stabilized!"

I sat up and took notice then, partly because the protein really had stabilized instead of degrading the way an unstable mutation does, partly because anything that excites Daniel Wallace that much is something to think about.

We watched the display like two cats at a mouse-hole, but it didn't change again. After a while a smaller structure did, though, and later in the night a whole procession of them transformed across the display and fell into place around the first one, forming a pattern that didn't make any sense to us. They stopped changing around midnight and we went to bed, but neither of us got to sleep right away.

"Maybe we ought to look for another interest in life ourselves instead of drumming up one for Emily," Daniel said. He meant it as a joke but it had a shaky sound; "Something besides getting intoxicated every night, for instance."

"You think we've got neural degradation from consuming flavor enhancers?" I asked.

Daniel laughed at that, sounding more like his old self. "No, Logan. No two people ever had instantaneous and identical hallucinations."

"Look," I said. "I know this sounds crazy but maybe Emily—"

Daniel wasn't amused any more. "Don't be a fool, Logan. If those proteins really mutated you can be sure of two things—Emily had nothing to do with it, and the news feeds will explain everything tomorrow."

He was wrong on one count at least.

The news feeds next day were packed with alerts three inches high but none of them explained anything. The broadcast commentators quoted every authority they could reach, and biotechnology experts were going crazy everywhere. It just couldn't happen, they said.

Daniel and I went over the news feed by feed that night and I learned more about protein structures than I'd learned in a lifetime. Daniel, as I've said before, is an educated man, and what he couldn't recall offhand about biotechnology the news feeds quoted by chapter and verse. They ran interviews with researchers at GeneTech Laboratories and BioSynth Corporation and MolecularDynamics Institute and God knows where else, but nobody could explain why all of those proteins would spontaneously mutate then stabilize.

It set me back on my heels to learn that hemoglobin was critical for oxygen transport and had a complex quaternary structure, that it was highly conserved across species and had variants that were more efficient than the standard but didn't occur naturally. This variant—researchers called it the "Enhanced" because hemoglobin was the blood protein—hadn't degraded, which puzzled the researchers no end. I suggested to Daniel, only half joking, that maybe the Enhanced had stayed stable because it wasn't complex enough to suit Emily's taste, but Daniel called me down sharp.

"Don't joke about Emily," he said sternly. "Getting back to hemoglobin—it's so fundamental that its genetic code has been conserved for millions of years. That means any mutation would have started when Emily was only eighteen months old. The laws of biochemistry are universal constants, Logan, and researchers say they can't be violated."

"They said the proteins couldn't be tossed around like building blocks, too," I pointed out. "I'm not saying that Emily really mutated those damn proteins, Daniel, but if she did she could have altered the entire biochemical pathway along with them, couldn't she?"

But Daniel wouldn't argue the point. "I'm going out for air," he said.

I trailed along, but we didn't get farther than Emily's hoverchair.

There she sat, tense and absorbed, staring up at the holographic display. Daniel and I followed her gaze, the way you do automatically when somebody ahead of you cranes their neck at something. We looked up just in time to see the proteins start mutating again.

The first one to go was a large complex one that transformed across the display like a cascade reaction—zip, like that—and stabilized beside the group that had mutated the night before.

Daniel said, "There went collagen," and his voice sounded like he had just run a mile.

That was only the beginning. During the next hour forty or fifty more proteins transformed across the display and joined the group that had mutated the night before. The pattern they made still didn't look like anything in particular.

I left Daniel shaking his head at the display and went over to give Emily, who had called it a night and was manually guiding her hoverchair toward the Gutierrez pod, a boost up the entrance ramp. I pushed her inside where Daniel couldn't hear, then I asked her how things were going.

"Slow, Logan," she said. "I've got 'most a hundred to go, yet."

"Then you're really mutating those proteins up there?"

She looked surprised. "Sure, it's not so hard once you know how."

The odds were even that she was pulling my leg, but I went ahead anyway and asked another question.

"I can't make head or tail of it, Emily," I said. "What're you making up there?"

She gave me a very small smile.

"You'll know when I'm through," she said.

I told Daniel about that after we'd bunked in, but he said I should not encourage the kid in her delusional thinking. "Emily's heard everybody talking about those proteins mutating, the broadcast commentators blared about it, so she's excited too. But she's got a lot more imagination than most people, because she's a disabled child, and she could develop a dangerous delusion because she's upset about Rita. The thing to do is give her a logical explanation instead of letting her think her fantasy is a fact."

Daniel was taking all this so hard—because it was upsetting things he'd taken for granted as being facts all his life, like those researchers who were going nuts in droves all over the colonies. I didn't realize how upset Daniel really was, though, till he woke me up at about 4:00 a.m.

"I can't sleep for thinking about those proteins," he said, sitting on the edge of my bunk. "Logan, I'm scared."

That from Daniel was something I'd never expected to hear. It startled me wide enough awake to sit up in the dark and listen while he unloaded his worries.

"I'm afraid," Daniel said, "because what is happening up there isn't right or natural. It just can't be, yet it is."

It was so quiet when he paused that I could hear the blood swishing in my ears. Finally Daniel said, "Logan, the biochemistry we depend on is as delicately balanced as a fine chronometer. If that balance is upset too far our world will be affected drastically."

Ordinarily I wouldn't have argued with Daniel on his own ground, but I could see he was painting a mental picture of the whole biosphere collapsing like a failed simulation and I was afraid to let him go on.

"The trouble with you educated people," I said, "is that you think your experts have got everything figured out, that there's nothing in the world their algorithms can't pin down. Well, I'm an illiterate worker, but I know that your researchers can measure the proteins till they're blue in the face and they'll never learn who designed those proteins there. So how do they know that whoever designed them there won't change them again? I've always heard that if a person had faith enough they could move mountains. Well, if a person has the faith in themselves that Emily's got maybe they could mutate proteins, too."

Daniel sat quiet for a minute.

"'There are more things, Horatio....'" he began, then laughed. "A line worn threadbare by centuries of repetition but as apt tonight as ever, Logan. Do you really believe Emily is mutating those proteins?"

"Why not?" I came back. "It's as good an answer as any the experts have come up with."

Daniel got up and went back to his own bunk. "Maybe you're right. We'll find out tomorrow."

And we did. Daniel did, rather, while I was hard at work engineering cellular structures in the depths of the lab.

I got home a little earlier than usual that night, just before it got really dark. Emily was sitting as usual all alone in her hoverchair. In the gloom I could see a stack of educational materials on the grass beside her, materials Daniel had given her to study. The thing that stopped me was that Emily was staring at her feet as if they were the first ones she'd ever seen, and she had the same look of intense concentration on her face that I'd seen when she was manipulating the proteins.

I didn't know what to say to her, thinking maybe I'd better not mention the proteins. But Emily spoke first.

"Logan," she said, without taking her eyes off her toes, "did you know that Daniel is an awfully wise man?"

I said I'd always thought so, but why?

"Daniel said this morning that I ought not to mutate any more proteins," the kid said. "He says I ought to concentrate instead on learning how to walk again so I can go off-world and find Rita."

For a minute I was mad enough to brain Daniel Wallace if he'd been handy. Anybody that would pull a gag like that on a disabled, helpless kid....

"Daniel says that if I can do what I've been doing to the proteins then it ought to be easy to repair my own nerve pathways," Emily said. "And he's right, Logan. So I'm not going to mutate any more proteins. I'm going to repair my nerve pathways."

She looked up at me with her small, solemn smile. "It took me a whole day to learn how to mutate that first protein, Logan, but I could do this after only a couple of hours. Look...."

And she wiggled the toes on both feet.

It's a pity things don't happen in life like they do in simulations, because a first-class story could be made out of Emily Gutierrez's knack for altering things by concentrating on them. In a simulation Emily might have saved the world or destroyed it, depending on which line would interest the most viewers and bring the creator the fattest credit, but of course it didn't really turn out either way. It ended in what Daniel Wallace called an anticlimax, leaving everybody happy enough except a few researchers who like mysteries anyway or they wouldn't be researchers in the first place.

The proteins that had been mutated stayed where they were, but the pattern they had started was never finished. That unfinished pattern won't ever go away, in case you've wondered about it—it's up there in the database where you can access it any clear cycle—but it will never be finished because Emily Gutierrez lost interest in it when she learned to walk again.

Walking was a slow business with Emily at first because her legs had got thin and weak—partially atrophied muscles, Daniel said—and it took time to make them round and strong again. But in a couple of weeks she was stumping around on support braces and after that she never went near her hoverchair again.

Camila sent her to school at Springfield District by transit and before vacation time came around she was playing sports and swimming in the recreation center with a gang of other kids on rest days.

School opened up a whole new world to Emily and she fitted herself into the routine as neat as if she'd been doing it all her life. She learned a lot there and she forgot a lot that she'd learned for herself by being alone. Before we realized what was happening she was just like any other ten-year-old, full of curiosity and energy, with no more power to alter things by concentrating on them than anybody else had.

I think she actually forgot about those proteins along with other things that had meant so much to her when she was confined to her hoverchair and couldn't do anything but wait and think.

For instance, a basic AI companion followed her home from Foxwood City one day and Camila let her keep it. She programmed the companion and customized it and named it Nova, and after that she never said anything more about going off-world to find Rita. It was only natural, of course, because kids—normal kids—forget their pain quickly. It's a sort of defense mechanism, Daniel says, against the disappointments of this life.

When school opened again in the fall Camila sold her pod and got a position in Springfield District where Emily could walk to school instead of going by transit. When they were gone the Foxwood City residential complex was so lonesome and dead that Daniel and I pulled out and went down to the Valleyview, Wendria sector for the agricultural biotech season. We never heard from Camila and Emily again.

We've moved several times since; we're out in the supply chain management facilities just now, with the logistics coordinators. But everywhere we go we're reminded of them. Every time we access the biochemistry database we see what Daniel calls the Emily Gutierrez Molecular Monument, which is nothing but a funny sort of pattern roughed in with a hundred or so proteins of all sizes and complexities.

The structure of it is so sketchy that you'd never make out what it's supposed to be unless you knew already what you were looking for. To us the head of an AI companion is fairly plain. If you know enough to fill in the gaps you can see it was meant to be a complex construct with only one optical sensor.

Daniel says that footloose workers like him and me forget old associations as quick as kids do—and for the same good reason—so I'm not especially interested now in where Camila and Emily Gutierrez are or how they're doing. But there's one thing I'll always wonder about, now that there's no way of ever knowing for sure.

I wish I'd asked Emily or Camila, before they moved away, how Rita lost that other sensor.
